slides.title: Parts of a letter
slides.text:
A friendly letter has parts:

1. **Greeting**: Dear Sara,
2. **Body**: your message
3. **Closing**: Your friend,
4. **Signature**: your name

slides.title: Commas in a letter
slides.text:
Put a **comma** after the greeting.

Dear Grandma**,**

Put a **comma** after the closing.

Love**,**

slides.title: Titles of people
slides.text:
Some short words go before a name. They start with a **capital letter** and end with a **period**.

**Mr.** Ali   **Mrs.** Huda   **Dr.** Salem

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To prove your answer:

1. Find the part of the letter the question asks about.
2. Look at **where** it is: the top, the middle or the end.
3. Point to that line.

example.explain: **Dear Uncle Saad,** is the greeting. It says who the letter is **to**, and it ends with a comma.

together.passage: Dear Grandpa, Thank you for the book about stars. I read it every night. Love, Omar
together.stem: Which part tells who wrote the letter?
options: Thank you for the book about stars.
together.hint: The writer signs the letter at the very end. Look at the last line.
together.good: Yes! **Omar** is the signature. It comes after the closing.

sentences: Thank you for the book about stars.
evidence.stem: The answer was: Omar wrote it. Tap the line that shows who wrote the letter.
evidence.wrong: This line does not tell who wrote the letter. Look at the very end.

checks.passage: Our teacher is mr. Hassan. He teaches us science.
checks.stem: How should the teacher's name be written?
checks.why: A title before a name starts with a capital letter: **Mr. Hassan**.

checks.passage: Dear Laila, I miss you. Please visit soon. Your friend, Reem
checks.why: The closing comes at the end, just before the name. **Your friend,** is the closing.

checks.passage:
Dear Ahmad
I had fun at your house. See you at school!
Your friend,
Khalid
checks.stem: What mark should come after "Dear Ahmad"?
checks.why: In a friendly letter, the greeting ends with a **comma**: Dear Ahmad,

again.title: Top, middle, end
again.text:
Think of a letter like a sandwich.

**Top**: Dear ...,
**Middle**: what you want to say
**End**: Love, or Your friend, and then your name.
again.example:
Dear Mama, ← top
I made you a card. ← middle
Love, Rania ← end

slides.title: What is an abbreviation?
slides.text:
An **abbreviation** is a short way to write a word.

Most start with a **capital letter** if the word does, and end with a **period**.

Street → **St.**
Monday → **Mon.**
January → **Jan.**

slides.title: Titles before names
slides.text:
**Mr.** = a man
**Mrs.** = a married woman
**Ms.** = a woman
**Dr.** = Doctor

They always start with a **capital** letter.

slides.title: The date in a letter
slides.text:
Write the date at the top of a letter.

Put a **comma** between the day and the year:

May 4**,** 2026

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To prove what an abbreviation means:

1. Find the short word in the text.
2. Read the lines around it for **clues**.
3. Point to the line with the abbreviation and the line with the clue.

sentences.t: Our new address is 12 Palm St.

example.explain: **St.** is the short form of **Street**. It begins with a capital letter and ends with a period.

together.passage: May 4, 2026 Dear Dr. Salem, Thank you for visiting our class on Monday. Your talk about healthy teeth was very interesting. Many of us now brush our teeth twice a day. Sincerely, Class 5B
together.stem: What does "Dr." stand for in this letter?
together.hint: Read the letter. What did the visitor talk about? What job fits that?
together.good: Yes! **Dr.** is short for **Doctor**. The talk about healthy teeth fits a doctor's job.

sentences: Thank you for visiting our class on Monday.
Your talk about healthy teeth was very interesting.
Many of us now brush our teeth twice a day.
evidence.stem: The answer was: Doctor. Tap 2 lines: the one with the abbreviation and the one that shows the visitor's job.
evidence.wrong: This line does not help. Find the line with Dr. and the line about what the visitor talked about.

checks.passage: Our family moved last week. Our new house is on Garden Street.
checks.stem: How do you write "Street" as an abbreviation?
checks.why: The short form of Street is **St.**: a capital S, a small t and a period.

checks.passage: Today is Thursday, March 5, 2026. Our class will plant trees.
checks.stem: Which is the correct abbreviation for this month?
checks.why: Month abbreviations start with a capital letter and end with a period: **Mar.**

checks.passage: The letter was addressed to Doctor Faisal Al-Qahtani.
checks.stem: Which is the correct short form?
checks.why: The title starts with a capital: **Dr.** The name keeps its capital letters too.

again.title: Short word, same start
again.text:
An abbreviation keeps the **first letters** of the word.

If the long word starts with a capital, the short one does too. Then add a period.

slides.title: A formal letter
slides.text:
A **formal letter** is written to someone you do not know well, like a manager or a principal.

It has a heading, a greeting, a body, a closing and a signature, just like a friendly letter, but the words are more polite and serious.

slides.title: Greeting and closing
slides.text:
In a formal letter, the greeting is often followed by a **colon**:

Dear Ms. Al-Harbi**:**

The closing has a **comma**, and only its **first word** has a capital letter:

Sincerely,   Yours truly,   Best regards,

slides.title: Units and short forms
slides.text:
Some abbreviations use **no period** and **no capital**:

km (kilometres)   cm   kg

Some use capitals with no periods, like **KSA**.

Always follow the usual form, not your own.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To find a mistake in a letter:

1. Check each part: greeting, body, closing, signature.
2. Check the punctuation and capitals in each part.
3. Point to the line that breaks a rule.

sentences.t: Thank you for your quick reply.

example.explain: In a closing, only the **first** word has a capital letter. **Best Regards,** should be **Best regards,**.

together.passage: Dear Ms. Al-Harbi: I am writing to ask whether our class may visit the city aquarium on Tuesday, April 14. We are studying ocean animals in science this term. There will be twenty-four students and three teachers. Please let us know if this date is possible. Yours Truly, Omar Saleh
options: Change the colon after the greeting to a period.
together.hint: Check the capital letters in each part. Which part should have only one capital?
together.good: Yes! Only the first word of a closing is capitalised: **Yours truly,**

sentences: I am writing to ask whether our class may visit the city aquarium on Tuesday, April 14.
We are studying ocean animals in science this term.
There will be twenty-four students and three teachers.
Please let us know if this date is possible.
evidence.stem: The answer was: the closing needs a small t. Tap the line with the mistake.
evidence.wrong: This line is written correctly. Find the line where a word has a capital it should not have.

checks.passage: Thank you for your help with our school project. [closing] Huda Ahmed
checks.stem: Which closing should go in the letter?
checks.why: A closing starts with a capital letter, has no other capitals and ends with a comma: **Sincerely,**

checks.passage: The new park is 3 kilometres from our school. Its walking track is 800 metres long.
checks.why: Units of measurement use small letters and no period: **km**.

checks.passage: Prof. Lina Saeed teaches chemistry at the university. Her students say her classes are hard but fair.
checks.why: **Prof.** is a title before a name. It is short for **Professor**, a university teacher.

again.title: Check one capital
again.text:
For a closing, remember: **one capital, one comma**.

Only the first word gets a capital letter. The closing ends with a comma.
again.example:
Yours sincerely,  ✓
Yours Sincerely,  ✗
yours sincerely,  ✗

slides.title: Formal means full
slides.text:
In the **body** of a formal letter, write most words **in full**.

Write **Wednesday, February 4**, not Wed., Feb. 4.

Titles before names, like **Dr.** and **Ms.**, and time marks like **p.m.** are still fine.

slides.title: Commas in dates and places
slides.text:
Use commas to separate the parts of a date and a place:

June 10**,** 2026
Abha**,** Saudi Arabia

In a sentence, add a comma **after** the last part too:

We met in Abha**,** Saudi Arabia**,** last year.

slides.title: Latin short forms
slides.text:
**e.g.** = for example
**i.e.** = that is (it explains exactly)
**etc.** = and so on

Do not mix them up: e.g. gives **some** examples; i.e. gives the **exact** meaning.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To revise a letter:

1. Read each line and ask: is it correct **and** formal?
2. Check abbreviations, capitals and commas against the rules.
3. Only change what breaks a rule. Point to that line.

sentences.t: Please bring a laptop, a notebook, etc.
We will finish on Thurs., Oct. 8.

example.explain: Times like **9:00 a.m.** are fine in a formal letter, and so is **etc.** But the day and month in the body should be written in full: **Thursday, October 8**.

together.passage: Al-Noor School, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia January 20, 2026 Dear Dr. Mansour: Our school would be honoured to welcome you as a guest speaker at our science evening. The event will take place on Wed., Feb. 4, from 6:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. in the school hall. Students will present projects on clean energy, e.g., solar panels and wind turbines. We would be grateful if you could reply by January 27. Sincerely, Maha Al-Otaibi, Science Coordinator
together.stem: Which change would make the letter correct and formal?
options: Write "Dr." in full in the greeting.
together.hint: Some short forms are fine in a formal letter. Which one should be written out in the body?
together.good: Yes! In the body of a formal letter, write the day and month in full: **Wednesday, February 4**.

sentences: Our school would be honoured to welcome you as a guest speaker at our science evening.
The event will take place on Wed., Feb. 4, from 6:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. in the school hall.
Students will present projects on clean energy, e.g., solar panels and wind turbines.
We would be grateful if you could reply by January 27.
evidence.stem: The answer was: write the day and month in full. Tap the line that needs this change.
evidence.wrong: This line already follows the rules. Find the line with a shortened day and month.

checks.passage: Our school has three sports teams, i.e., football, basketball and volleyball.
checks.stem: What does "i.e." mean in this sentence?
checks.why: **i.e.** means "that is". It tells you exactly which three teams the school has.

checks.passage: The letter was sent from Abha Saudi Arabia on June 10 2026.
checks.why: Commas separate the city from the country and the day from the year, with one after the country too: **from Abha, Saudi Arabia, on June 10, 2026.**

checks.passage: My aunt is a dr. at the city hospital. She works long hours.
checks.stem: What is wrong in the first sentence?
checks.why: Dr. is used only as a title **before a name**. On its own, write the word in full: **doctor**.

again.title: Ask: is it before a name?
again.text:
Many abbreviations are allowed in only one place.

**Dr.**, **Mr.**, **Ms.**: only right before a name.
**Days and months**: write them in full in a formal letter's body.
again.example:
Dear **Dr.** Mansour ✓
She is a **dr.** ✗ → She is a **doctor**.
On **Wed.** ✗ → On **Wednesday**.
